**Question 3 of up to 5**

**Question:** Should the "output file would be its own input" check run for all inputs up front, before anything is written, or only when the tool reaches the offending input? (FR-020)

**Why it matters:** The spec's example has one input file, so the answer doesn't show. With several inputs it does: running `--out-dir out a.log out/b.log` means `out/b.log` is both an input and a destination. Checking up front means the run fails having written nothing; checking on arrival means `out/a.log` is already written and kept when the tool exits 2. Both are defensible, but they need different tests, and only one matches FR-015.

**Recommended:** Option A - FR-015 already establishes the pattern of proving the destination usable before consuming any input, precisely so a doomed run doesn't leave a half-done folder. Extending that to the collision check is consistent, and comparing resolved paths for every input up front is one loop rather than a check threaded through the write path.

| Option | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| A | Pre-flight: before reading any input, check every FILE against the output path it would produce. Any collision fails immediately — nothing read, nothing written, exit 2. |
| B | On arrival: process inputs in order and fail when the colliding one is reached, keeping output files already completed for earlier inputs. |
| Short | Provide a different short answer (<=5 words) |

You can reply with the option letter (e.g., "A"), accept the recommendation by saying "yes" or "recommended", or provide your own short answer.
